extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, and editors of classical mathematics texts (Archimedes)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and substantive criteria for producing a critical/friendly edition of Archimedes’ works (text reproduction, editorial apparatus, and manuscript evaluation), plus descriptive criteria for understanding Archimedes’ method and presentation. Useful for editors, textual critics, and historians of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful reproduction of the treatises
rubrics_metrics.description: Present a perfectly faithful reproduction of the treatises as they have come down to us, neither adding anything nor leaving out anything essential or important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author’s main object: faithful reproduction; avoid additions or omissions that alter substance. (Preface: “My main object has been to present a perfectly faithful reproduction of the treatises as they have come down to us, neither adding anything nor leaving out anything essential or important.”)

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain original numbering and near-original enunciation of propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain the numbering of the propositions and enunciate them in a manner more nearly approaching the original without thereby making the enunciations obscure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible keep original proposition numbering; reformulate enunciations only so far as necessary for clarity but avoid obscuring original structure. (Preface: explains less need for compression than with Apollonius and the decision to retain numbering.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure reasonable uniformity of notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to secure as much uniformity in the notation used as is fairly possible, but not at the cost of obscuring readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform notation is desirable (helps readability), but absolute uniformity is not mandatory if it would make the text less clear; balance fidelity to originals with the reader’s comprehension. (Preface: contrasted with necessity for Apollonius.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purposes and placement of editorial notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes should chiefly throw light on particular points in the text or supply proofs of propositions assumed by Archimedes as known; occasionally insert short notes in square brackets after propositions (in same type) to bring out exact significance where footnotes/introduction might be overlooked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use notes to illuminate and to supply missing proofs; when a clarification must not be missed, place it immediately after the proposition in brackets and same type rather than buried in the introduction or footnotes. (Preface: explicit practice described.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction structure: historical material and methods separated
rubrics_metrics.description: Make much of the Introduction historical; devote the rest partly to a general view of certain methods employed by Archimedes and of their mathematical significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate documentary/historical presentation from methodological discussion; give readers both the authentic historical record and a synthetic account of methods and significance for modern readers. (Preface: describes this plan.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about speculative hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: When it is necessary to put forward hypotheses for explaining obscure points where no positive historical data exist, call attention to their speculative character and give the historical evidence where such can be quoted in support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between authentic information and conjectural inference; explicitly label speculative hypotheses and supply whatever supporting evidence exists so readers can judge probability. (Preface: author’s explicit caution.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Include reasonably complete treatment of related/auxiliary topics when justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a related subject is interesting and helps round off the study, give a more complete account even if it goes somewhat beyond what is strictly necessary for elucidation of Archimedes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide supplementary chapters (e.g., on inclinationes) when they materially aid understanding or complete the scholarly treatment; justify length by scholarly usefulness. (Preface: author defends a long chapter on inclinationes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid including portraits or illustrations without authoritative provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not place a portrait claiming to represent Archimedes unless there is sufficient authority for the identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate iconographic authority before including a portrait; omit if no recognized authority exists to avoid misleading readers. (Preface: decision not to include a portrait after enquiries.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge contributions of proofreaders and collaborators
rubrics_metrics.description: Credit those who read proof sheets and assisted editorially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize scholarly assistance (e.g., proof-reading, commentary) in prefatory acknowledgments; useful for transparency and scholarly record. (Preface: thanks to proof-reader brother.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine manuscript archetype, origin, and dating
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish whether a set of MSS. derives from a common archetype and attempt to date that archetype (e.g., as early as 9th or 10th century) by paleographic and other evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use paleography (letter-forms, abbreviations), internal notes, and historical references to estimate archetype dating. (Chapter II: discussion of Valla MS and inferred 9th/10th-century archetype.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace manuscript provenance via ownership notes and documentary clues
rubrics_metrics.description: Use notes about previous owners (e.g., George Valla, Alberto Pio, Cardinal Rodolphus Pius) and contemporary letters to trace a manuscript’s history and infer relationships among copies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correlate marginalia, ownership inscriptions, and external documentary evidence (letters, inventories) to reconstruct provenance and transmission history. (Chapter II: multiple examples cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare shared lacunae, readings, abbreviations and errors to infer copying relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Infer derivation between MSS. by examining common lacunae, identical corruptions, shared lists of abbreviations, and the order/contents of books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically collate readings: shared defects (e.g., same missing pages), identical corruptions, and matching abbreviations are evidence of common archetype or direct descent; divergent corrections may signal later interpolations. (Chapter II: F, B, C comparison, lacuna concordance.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess relative trustworthiness of MSS by concordance with translations and paleographic features
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge a manuscript’s trustworthiness by its agreement with early translations and by internal paleographic markers (e.g., letter-forms older than a certain century, faithful copying of figures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a manuscript corresponds with independent early translations (e.g., Valla’s translations) and shows conservative paleography and careful copyist practices, treat it as more reliable. (Chapter II: reasons for considering F most trustworthy.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use external documentary evidence (letters, editions, translator notes) to support textual history
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ letters, early printed editions, translator notes, and similar documentary sources to place manuscripts and translations in chronological context and to support reconstruction of archetypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correlate mentions in correspondence (e.g., Politianus, Regiomontanus), early translations, and catalogue notes to confirm dating and relationships. (Chapter II: multiple documentary examples used.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide exhaustive bibliography / list of principal works consulted
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a list of principal works consulted—editions, commentaries, histories—to support editorial decisions and further research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comprehensive bibliography supports claims, traces scholarly lineage, and assists readers who wish to verify or deepen understanding. (Preface: long list of works consulted.)

rubrics_metrics.name: State order and contents of collected works clearly, including fragments and commentaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Declare which works and fragments are included, their order, and any additional materials (e.g., Eutocius’ commentaries, Heron’s fragments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit the contents and arrangement of the edition so readers know what is included and how the collection corresponds to manuscript groups. (Chapter II: F, B, C contents enumerated.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of Archimedes’ mathematical method and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes’ method is deliberate: he approaches problems with a sequence of propositions whose immediate bearing may not appear but are used later — a stepwise, highly finished development where each step depends on preceding ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the rhetorical and methodological feature that proofs are elaborated and preparatory propositions may obscure how the discoverer originally conceived the solution; editors/commentators should elucidate this tactic for modern readers. (Preface: discussion of Archimedes’ deliberation and ‘covering up the traces’.)
